caseName: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
legalIssue: Constitutionality of Section 66A of IT Act; standards for digital communication offenses and online threats.
summary: Landmark ruling striking down vague digital speech provisions while clarifying procedures for legitimate intermediary takedowns and electronic harassment investigations.
courtReasoning: The Court distinguished between mere discussion, advocacy, and clear incitement/threat. For actionable digital offenses, an overt act of intimidation or deceptive inducement under specific statutory provisions must be established.
outcome: Guidelines issued for digital speech, online intimidation complaints, and police registration criteria.
sourceDocument: Supreme Court Law Reports (Illustrative Mock Record)

caseName: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal
legalIssue: Admissibility of electronic records and mandatory certificate requirement under electronic evidence rules.
summary: Authoritative decision on the necessity of electronic certification for digital records, SMS, chat transcripts, and server logs produced in court.
courtReasoning: The Supreme Court clarified that production of an electronic certificate is a condition precedent to the admissibility of secondary electronic evidence (such as printouts of chats and screenshots) to prevent tampering.
outcome: Strict guidelines on digital chain of custody; reflected in Section 61/63 of Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
sourceDocument: Supreme Court Case Database (Illustrative Mock Record)

caseName: State of Maharashtra v. Mohd. Afzal (Cyber Fraud & Account Takeover)
legalIssue: Simultaneous application of penal law (cheating/intimidation) and IT Act provisions in social media account takeover and extortion.
summary: Accused hacked social media profiles, locked out original owners, and demanded ransom while threatening to circulate altered photographs.
courtReasoning: The High Court held that hacking an account and subsequently extorting or intimidating the victim constitutes distinct and cumulative offences under both IT Act (Sec 66/66C) and penal code provisions (BNS 318/351 / IPC 420/506).
outcome: Conviction upheld; clear precedent on handling combined hacking + extortion grievances.
sourceDocument: Bombay High Court Law Reports (Illustrative Mock Record)

caseName: Ramesh Kumar v. State of NCT of Delhi (UPI & QR Code Deception)
legalIssue: Deceiving victims through fraudulent payment links and fake QR codes under penal cheating and identity impersonation.
summary: Victim was deceived into scanning a reverse QR code believing they were receiving money for online sale of household items.
courtReasoning: The Court observed that inducement through malicious payment gateways directly constitutes dishonest inducement under Cheating provisions (BNS 318 / IPC 420) along with IT Act Section 66D for digital impersonation.
outcome: Bail rejected; immediate bank freezing under procedural provisions (BNSS 107) affirmed.
sourceDocument: Delhi High Court Judgments (Illustrative Mock Record)
